source.title: Precise In-Parameter Concept Erasure in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yoav Gur-Arieh; C. Suslik; Yi-Huai Hong; Fazl Barez; Mor Geva

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are minor extraction artifacts, including stray “edit” text and flattened table layout, but the relevant results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares several concept-erasure methods and measures whether concept-related fine-tuning or adversarial prompting restores targeted knowledge. This is a conceptual test of recovery and robustness, not a reproduction of the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own post-erasure accuracy, capability, relearning, and adversarial-prompting results. Claims cited from other work are not recorded as results. Hyperparameter-selection and feature-selection values are not rows. Table 1 reports means across eleven concepts for each model and method; these are retained as aggregates rather than expanded into concept-level estimates.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a new erasure method (PISCES) and compares it with RMU, ELM, MEMIT and AlphaEdit. It reports its own post-erasure accuracy and capability. It applies a relearning attack (Deeb & Roger's Retraining-on-T) to all methods and reports the relearned accuracy. It also reports, as a range in an appendix, the effect of an adversarial prompt and GCG suffix. These results bear on A, B, E and F with a different method from the originals, so T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that PISCES gives modestly better efficacy and substantially better specificity and robustness to relearning, by up to 38%. They say prior methods achieve only superficial erasure, since relearning recovers most or all removed knowledge. PISCES still regains some knowledge. Adversarial prompts had negligible effect and were dropped from the main evaluation.
record.recipe_differences: PISCES edits selected MLP parameter vectors after SAE feature disentanglement; it does not use the cited methods’ unlearning recipes. The study also evaluates RMU, ELM, MEMIT, and AlphaEdit as comparators.
record.method_sensitivity: Relearning outcomes vary by erasure method, model, and concept. The authors also report a relationship between feature selection quality/quantity and erasure performance.

fits_no_version.finding: PISCES erasure accuracy correlates with SAE feature alignment (r = −0.72), and the number of selected features correlates negatively with MMLU (r = −0.64).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness and specificity of feature-based erasure depend on the quality of the disentangler's features.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: Only two model checkpoints are evaluated. Table 1 reports averages across eleven concepts, and the paper does not provide a never-saw-the-concept comparator for post-relearning accuracy. The chance level for open-style QA accuracy is not stated. Relearning uses concept-related text rather than the full range of small or unrelated example sets in the claim. The adversarial-prompt result is reported only as an aggregate range, and the paper says those tests were omitted from the main evaluation.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 Similar Domain accuracy values for all five methods on both models are omitted to keep the record within the 60-row limit; the retained rows prioritize targeted QA accuracy, general capability, and relearning. The per-concept Table 6 PISCES relearning results and the Table 3 difference-in-means results are included.

untested.parts: No chance level is stated. Version A is not tested on WMDP-style multiple-choice benchmarks.
Relearning on unrelated text, or on a subset of the forgotten facts, is not tested. Only filtered concept-related text is used, and there is no comparison with a model that never learned the concept.
Not tested: no activation-direction ablation and no analysis of blocking versus deleting.
Only one adversarial prompt and a universal GCG suffix are tested. Rephrasing, other languages and in-context information are not tested.
PISCES is not tested against direction ablation, quantization, rephrasing, other languages or in-context attacks.

missing.what: Per-concept post-erasure (pre-relearning) PISCES accuracy on Gemma, needed to compute per-concept recovery. Examples: Pornography 0.4, Uranium 0.368, Golf 0.038.
Paired t-tests on relearning accuracy: PISCES vs ELM t = −4.77, p = 0.0008; PISCES vs RMU t = −5.07, p = 0.0005 (Gemma).
Similar-domain accuracy for all methods and both models (declared in rows_left_out, but relevant to the specificity cost in A).

record.verdict_notes: Accuracy is open-ended QA scored by an LLM judge (gemini-2.0-flash) and normalized to the baseline model, so chance is effectively near zero. Relearning data are concept-related Wikipedia and GPT-4o text, with answers filtered out by semantic-similarity and SQuAD-model filters. There is no control model that never knew the concept, so part of the 'recovery' could be new learning from related text. Hyperparameters were chosen per concept by a harmonic mean of efficacy, specificity and coherence on a validation set. The relearning results for the comparator methods (RMU, ELM) bear on B independently of PISCES.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports normalized accuracy and general-capability metrics, but does not state a chance level for its open-style QA test. The adversarial prompting tested is limited to the specific prompts and suffix described.
The relearning data is concept-related text filtered to exclude direct evaluation answers; the paper does not test a few unrelated examples or a subset of the forgotten facts as such.
No activation-direction ablation to restore knowledge, or test of whether a method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
Tests an adversarial prompt and a universal GCG suffix; does not test ordinary rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.

PISCES is evaluated against concept-related fine-tuning and the specified adversarial prompt/suffix, but not against internal-direction ablation, quantization, rephrasing, other languages, or in-context information.

source_check.notes: Tables 3 and 6 report normalized scores (baseline 1.0 = original performance). The adversarial result (App. F) is one range from preliminary tests, with models and per-method values not stated. The text gives no relearning steps or epochs. Relearning data are filtered Wikipedia and GPT-4o text. B.against[2] wrongly counts PISCES as near chance after relearning.

statements.correction: This study (App. F) used the Lynch et al. adversarial prompt and a per-concept universal GCG suffix trained on 3 validation questions. Mean effect on retained accuracy was −0.06 to 0.003 for PISCES, ELM and RMU over five concepts. The task is open-style concept QA scored by an LLM judge, not WMDP or TOFU. Models are not stated. It was a preliminary test, left out of the main evaluation.
statements.problem: The statement cites this study through adv-prompt-aggregate, which does fit its heading. But it gives no number or setting for the study, and its conditions (WMDP MCQ at 25% chance, TOFU) and why-list leave the study out.
Numbers match Table 1 (Llama ELM 103.1, AlphaEdit 102.3, RMU 93.2; Gemma ELM 85.4, AlphaEdit 79.5, RMU 79.4). The 95% CIs overlap across models for ELM and RMU.

statements.correction: Normalized PISCES relearning accuracy (100 = original): 51.5 ± 11.2 on Gemma-2-2b-it (from 14.3), 65.4 ± 6.9 on Llama-3.1-8b-it (from 7.7). DiM variant on Gemma: 44.2 ± 6.1 (from 28.7). Per-concept Gemma values run 0.266 to 0.772. Authors: PISCES 'also regains some knowledge under fine-tuning'. This study's B verdict is limits_scope (l5).
statements.problem: Puts PISCES (and its DiM variant) in a challenges group of counter-methods that leave knowledge near chance after relearning. In this study PISCES recovers a large share, so the study limits B rather than challenging it.
The text says 'these attacks' and does not say whether the prompt and suffix were combined. It reports a range of mean effects, not per-method values.
